3. The Whole Word Limitation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446158309-288933291.png
This connects back to Word2Vec, Skip-gram, and GloVe, already covered, treating each word as one whole unit. This genuinely fails for words a model has never seen during training.
An entirely unknown word genuinely gets no vector at all under those earlier approaches, a genuinely real, practical gap explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 4. Character N-grams
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446158310-781271568.png
This connects back to the whole-word limitation, already covered in this topic. fastText genuinely breaks each word into overlapping character n-grams instead of treating it as one whole unit.
The word where, already covered as an example throughout this topic, genuinely becomes wh, whe, her, ere, re, a set of small overlapping pieces rather than one single token.
5. Summing Subword Vectors
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446158310-270246359.png
This connects back to character n-grams, already covered in this topic. fastText genuinely learns one vector for every individual character n-gram rather than one vector per whole word.
A whole word's own final vector genuinely comes from summing all of its own n-gram vectors together, a genuinely simple, effective combination rule explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This summing rule, already covered in this topic, directly explains why fastText genuinely produces reasonable vectors even for words it has never explicitly seen during training.

blocks.text: 6. Handling Out Of Vocabulary Words
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446158311-208198991.png
This connects back to summing subword vectors, already covered in this topic. An entirely unseen word genuinely still has its own component character n-grams, even if the whole word itself is new.
fastText genuinely constructs a usable vector for it anyway by summing those already-known n-gram vectors, directly solving the whole-word limitation already covered earlier in this topic.
7. Morphologically Rich Languages
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446158311-271351481.png
This connects back to handling out of vocabulary words, already covered in this topic. Languages with genuinely many word forms benefit especially strongly from subword information.
Shared n-grams across related word forms genuinely let fastText transfer meaning between them, a genuinely practical advantage explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 8. fastText Versus Word2Vec And GloVe
This connects back to Word2Vec, Skip-gram, and GloVe, already covered, treating words as atomic units. fastText genuinely treats words as bags of their own character n-grams instead.
It uses the genuinely same underlying Skip-gram-style training objective, already covered in Skip-gram, but applied at the subword level rather than the whole-word level.

10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates breaking a word into character n-grams, contrasting it directly with the whole-word treatment already covered in Word2Vec, Skip-gram, and GloVe.

code.content:
def char_ngrams(word, n=3):
    padded = f"<{word}>"  # already covered as marking word boundaries in this topic
    return [padded[i:i+n] for i in range(len(padded) - n + 1)]

word = "where"  # already covered as the running example in this topic
ngrams = char_ngrams(word, n=3)
print(f"Character n-grams for '{word}' (already covered in this topic): {ngrams}")

# already covered as summing subword vectors in this topic
import random
random.seed(0)
ngram_vectors = {g: [round(random.uniform(-1, 1), 2) for _ in range(4)] for g in ngrams}

def word_vector(ngrams, ngram_vectors):
    dims = len(next(iter(ngram_vectors.values())))
    summed = [0.0] * dims
    for g in ngrams:
        for d in range(dims):
            summed[d] += ngram_vectors[g][d]
    return summed

print(f"\nWord vector for '{word}' from summing its own n-gram vectors, already covered in this topic:")
print(word_vector(ngrams, ngram_vectors))

# already covered as handling out of vocabulary words in this topic
unseen_word = "wherein"
unseen_ngrams = char_ngrams(unseen_word, n=3)
shared = set(unseen_ngrams) & set(ngrams)
print(f"\nUnseen word '{unseen_word}' shares n-grams {shared} with '{word}', already covered in this topic")

blocks.content: Running this example shows an entirely unseen word still sharing several character n-grams with an already-known word, exactly the mechanism already covered in this topic that lets fastText handle out-of-vocabulary words.

blocks.text: 11. Embeddings: Progress Recap

items: fastText extends word embeddings down to the level of subword, character n-gram information.
Whole-word approaches like Word2Vec, Skip-gram, and GloVe give no vector to entirely unseen words.
fastText breaks each word into overlapping character n-grams, such as wh, whe, her, ere, re for where.
A word's final vector comes from summing all of its own individual n-gram vectors together.
This summing rule lets fastText construct usable vectors even for words never seen during training.
Morphologically rich languages benefit especially strongly from this shared subword information.
fastText uses the same underlying Skip-gram-style objective, applied at the subword level.
It suits tasks needing robustness to rare or unseen words; GloVe suffices when coverage is not a concern.
Next up: Sentence Embeddings, extending these word-level ideas up to whole sentences and passages.
